title: Rubio Says Washington Is Planning a Trump Visit to India Early Next Year. He'll Fly Out First to Set It Up.
excerpt: The Secretary of State told Indian media the US is 'on the last inches' of a trade deal and expects to visit New Delhi himself before year-end — but the relationship has a year's worth of bruises to show for the delay.
body:
Rubio Plans His Own Trip to New Delhi to "Set Up" the Visit

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told IANS at the White House that Washington is "working towards sometime early next year" to bring President Donald Trump to India — the first such trip since the February 2020 "Namaste Trump" spectacle in Ahmedabad that drew more than 100,000 people.

In the same interview, Rubio said he expects to fly to New Delhi himself before the end of 2026 to lay the groundwork, and added that a Quad leaders' summit — grouping the US, India, Japan and Australia — could convene "very soon."

"India is such a close partner and ally of the United States, and the relationship between the Prime Minister and the President couldn't be closer, which I think is really important in diplomacy," Rubio said.

The signal from America's top diplomat arrives at a moment when the India–US relationship is, by any honest measure, under strain.


![White House — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg/3840px-White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg)



> **"Rubio himself visited India last month in what officials described as a "repair" mission."**



## A Year of Friction — and Three Dead Sailors

Washington slapped steep tariffs on Indian goods over the past year, partly in retaliation for New Delhi's continued purchases of Russian oil. The US drew closer to Pakistan, a move that rankled Indian strategists. And then came the Gulf: three Indian merchant sailors were killed in strikes on commercial vessels by the US Navy during the Iran–Hormuz conflict — an incident that sent a chill through a bilateral relationship that rarely produces casualties on either side.

Rubio himself visited India last month in what officials described as a "repair" mission. He left without a public trade deal but did, apparently, leave with enough goodwill to begin planning a presidential visit.

## The Trade Deal Is in Its "Last Inches"

Both sides have been negotiating an interim Bilateral Trade Agreement since February, when they agreed to 18 per cent tariffs on Indian goods — lower than what Vietnam and Bangladesh face. But the deal stalled after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping global tariff regime, and a Section 301 probe into alleged overcapacity and forced labour in India further clouded talks.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer flew to New Delhi last week for two days of talks. India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking at the India Global Forum in London, said the contours of the agreement had been "ironed out" but New Delhi would not sign until Washington guaranteed a clear tariff edge over regional competitors.

"The whole deal was centred around that competitive advantage," Goyal said. "That 18 per cent over our neighbours and competing countries. That is why the deal was attractive for us."

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, in a separate interview at the White House, said only a "handful of issues" remain, most of them about the legal language of the final text. "We've been working on this deal for a year and a half. The European Union deal, which is still not done, is 20 years," Gor said.

A deadline looms: Washington's temporary 10 per cent tariff on a broad set of trading partners expires on July 24. If the deal is not sealed before then, the tariff landscape shifts again — and India's competitive edge may narrow.

## What It Means If You Live Between Both Countries

For the 4.4 million Indian Americans and the millions more who hold H-1B and green-card applications in bureaucratic limbo, a presidential visit to India is more than ceremony. It is the clearest signal that the bilateral mood is warm enough to sustain cooperation on the things that directly affect diaspora life: visa processing speeds, consular backlogs, the tone of enforcement, and the willingness of both governments to make the human plumbing of the relationship work.

The February 2020 visit produced a defence cooperation agreement, a $3 billion helicopter deal, and a general warmth that made the subsequent pandemic-era repatriation flights politically easier. A 2027 visit, if it happens, would land in the middle of US midterm-election season and just ahead of several Indian state elections — giving both leaders reason to show the relationship is delivering.

Rubio's framing was unambiguous: "We're on the last inches of getting it done and it's very positive." Whether those inches close before the visit — or become the visit's centrepiece — will shape the next chapter of a relationship that 37 million diaspora Indians are watching from both ends.
